overview.headline: Lift grows with wing area and pressure while staying perpendicular to flight

keyPoints.point: Lift generated depends on object size through pressure variation around body
keyPoints.quote: The amount of lift generated by an object depends on the size of the object.

keyPoints.point: Aerodynamic force equals pressure times surface area surrounding body
keyPoints.quote: The total aerodynamic force is equal to the pressure times the surface area around the body.

keyPoints.point: Lift acts as perpendicular component of aerodynamic force relative to flight direction
keyPoints.quote: Lift is the component of this force perpendicular to the flight direction.

keyPoints.point: Designers increase wing area during takeoff and landing at low velocity to keep lift high
keyPoints.quote: Takeoff and landing are times of relatively low velocity, so to keep the lift high (to avoid the ground!) designers try to increase the wing area.

keyTerms.gloss: perpendicular component of aerodynamic force that supports flight
keyTerms.quote: Lift is the component of this force perpendicular to the flight direction.

keyTerms.gloss: total force generated by pressure acting on surface area around body
keyTerms.quote: The total aerodynamic force is equal to the pressure times the surface area around the body.

keyTerms.gloss: flat projection of wing viewed from above looking along lift direction
keyTerms.quote: The planform area is the area of the wing as viewed from above the wing, looking along the “lift” direction.

keyTerms.gloss: value calculated from measured lift and area used to compare reference area choices
keyTerms.quote: the lift coefficient is determined experimentally, by measuring the lift and measuring the area

keyTerms.gloss: panels moved backwards to increase wing area during low velocity phases
keyTerms.quote: This is done by sliding the flaps backwards along metal tracks and shifting the slats forward to increase the wing area.
